steps.instruction: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wiring.
details: Find the USB-C cable that goes into the XIAO board.
Pull it out of the board (hold the plug, not the wire).
Lay the cable to one side - you will plug it back in at step 12.
Clear a space on the table so small parts don't roll away.
steps.look_for: Nothing is plugged into the board and no light is on.
steps.watch_out: Changing wires while the board has power can short a pin and damage the board.

steps.instruction: This is a breadboard. It lets us connect parts without soldering.
details: Turn the breadboard so the long edges run left to right.
Find the red + line and the blue − line along the top edge - these are the power rails.
Find the same two rails along the bottom edge.
Find the numbers 1, 5, 10 … across the top: these number the columns.
Find the letters a to j down the left side: these name the rows.
steps.look_for: Two rails at the top, two at the bottom, and a groove (the centre gap) across the middle.
steps.watch_out: Some breadboards split each rail in the middle - if yours has a gap in the red/blue line, treat the halves as separate.

steps.instruction: In each column, the five holes a–e are joined underneath - and so are f–j.
details: Put your finger on column 10, row a.
Slide down to row e: those five holes are one connection.
Cross the centre gap to row f: f to j is a different connection.
Each long rail row (+ or −) is joined all the way along.
steps.look_for: You can say which holes are joined: same column, same side of the gap.
steps.watch_out: Holes in the same ROW (left to right) are NOT joined - only columns and rails are.

concept.title: Connected strips
concept.text: Metal clips under each column join a–e together and f–j together. The centre gap separates them.

steps.instruction: Press the XIAO across the centre gap, USB-C end at the left, pins in columns 1–7.
details: Hold the XIAO with the USB-C socket pointing LEFT and the chip facing up.
Line up the left-most pins with column 1 - one row of pins above the gap, one below.
Check the pin labels: the top row reads 5V, GND, 3V3, D10, D9, D8, D7; the bottom row reads D0 to D6.
Press down gently and evenly with two fingers until the pins sink in.
Leave the holes above and below the board in each column free - you'll use them next.
steps.look_for: The board sits flat across the gap; no pin is bent; D0 is the bottom-left pin.
steps.watch_out: Never press a board in along one row only - both rows of pins in the same strip would short every pin together.

steps.instruction: Black wire: from the GND column (above the board) to the top − rail.
details: Find GND: the second pin from the left on the TOP row (column 2).
Push one end of a black jumper wire into a free hole in column 2 ABOVE the board.
Push the other end into the blue − rail along the top edge.
Tug gently - both ends should stay put.
steps.look_for: A black wire from column 2 (above the XIAO) into the top blue − rail.
steps.watch_out: Use the blue − rail, not the red + rail - mixing them up connects ground to power.

steps.instruction: Black wire: join the top − rail to the bottom − rail at column 24.
details: Take a second black jumper wire.
Push one end into the top blue − rail near column 24.
Run it down the right side and push the other end into the bottom blue − rail near column 24.
Now both − rails are ground.
steps.look_for: A black wire running straight down the right side, rail to rail.
steps.watch_out: Blue to blue only. If one end lands in a red + rail, move it.

steps.instruction: Find the LED's long leg. The long leg is the positive (+) side.
details: Hold the LED with its legs pointing down.
Compare the two legs: one is longer. That is + (the anode).
Feel the rim of the red dome: one side is flat. The leg on the flat side is − (the cathode).
Keep holding it this way for the next steps.
steps.look_for: You can point to the long (+) leg and the short (−) leg.
steps.watch_out: An LED only lights one way round. If the legs were trimmed, use the flat edge to find −.

steps.instruction: Yellow wire: from the D0 column (below the board) to column 12, row j.
details: Find D0: the bottom-left pin of the XIAO (column 1).
Push one end of the yellow jumper wire into a free hole in column 1 BELOW the board (row j).
Push the other end into column 12, row j.
Column 12 is now connected to pin D0.
steps.look_for: A yellow wire from column 1 (below the XIAO) to column 12, row j.
steps.watch_out: Stay on the bottom half (rows f–j) for both ends - the top half of column 12 is a different connection.

steps.instruction: LED: long leg in column 12, short leg in column 13 (row h).
details: Hold the LED long leg on the left.
Push the LONG leg into column 12, row h - the same column as the yellow wire.
Push the SHORT leg into column 13, row h.
The LED should stand up straight with the red dome on top.
steps.look_for: LED legs in 12 and 13, long leg in 12.
steps.watch_out: Long leg in 13 by mistake? The LED won't light - swap the legs.

steps.instruction: Resistor: from column 13 (row j) to the bottom − rail.
details: Find the 220 Ω resistor: its colour bands are red, red, brown (then gold).
Bend both legs down so they fit the holes.
Push one leg into column 13, row j - the same column as the LED's short leg.
Push the other leg into the bottom blue − rail.
Either way round is fine: resistors have no + or −.
steps.look_for: Resistor from column 13 into the bottom − rail.
steps.watch_out: Don't skip the resistor: without it too much current flows and the LED (or the pin) can burn out.

concept.title: Why a resistor?
concept.text: It limits the current through the LED to a safe few milliamps.

steps.instruction: Check the whole path with an adult before power: D0 → yellow wire → LED + … LED − → resistor → − rail → black wire → GND.
details: Trace with your finger from D0 along the yellow wire to column 12.
Up through the LED's long leg, out of its short leg into column 13.
Through the resistor into the bottom − rail.
Along the rail-to-rail black wire, up to the top − rail, and through the first black wire to GND.
Count: 3 wires, 1 LED, 1 resistor, the XIAO - nothing else on the board.
steps.look_for: One unbroken loop from D0 back to GND.
steps.watch_out: If any part touches a red + rail, move it before you plug in.

steps.instruction: Plug the USB-C data cable into the XIAO, then into the computer.
details: Plug the small USB-C end into the XIAO.
Plug the other end into your computer.
A small light on the XIAO may flicker - that's normal.
steps.look_for: The board has power (a tiny on-board light may glow).
steps.watch_out: Use a DATA cable - some cables only charge and the computer won't see the board.

steps.instruction: The program switches pin D0 on, waits half a second, switches it off, waits - forever.
details: Read the first line: const int LED = D0; gives pin D0 a name.
setup() runs once: pinMode makes D0 an output.
loop() runs forever: HIGH turns D0 on (3.3 V), LOW turns it off (0 V).
delay(500) waits 500 milliseconds - half a second.
steps.look_for: You can say what each of the 4 important lines does.
steps.watch_out: Real Tender Cells firmware never waits with delay(); it uses timers so it can keep listening for E-STOP. For a first blink, delay() keeps it simple.

concept.title: GPIO
concept.text: A general-purpose pin the program can switch on (3.3 V) or off (0 V).

steps.instruction: Upload the sketch from the Arduino IDE.
details: Open the Arduino IDE and paste the program from the last step into a new sketch.
Tools → Board → esp32 → XIAO_ESP32S3 (install the esp32 boards package first if it isn't listed).
Tools → USB CDC On Boot → Enabled.
Tools → Port → choose the port that appeared when you plugged in.
Click Upload (the → arrow) and wait for "Done uploading".
steps.look_for: "Done uploading" at the bottom of the IDE.
steps.watch_out: No port? Try another cable or USB socket. Still nothing: hold B (boot), tap R (reset), release B, then upload again.

steps.instruction: Watch the LED: on for half a second, off for half a second.
details: Look at the red LED on the breadboard.
Count: on, off, on, off - about once a second.
Change 500 to 100 in both delays and upload again: it blinks faster.
steps.look_for: A steady blink, about once a second.
steps.watch_out: Nothing changes when you edit the delays? You probably didn't upload - click Upload again.

steps.instruction: Not blinking? Check the LED direction, the resistor and both black wires.
details: Unplug the USB cable first.
LED: long leg in column 12 (with the yellow wire)? If not, turn it round.
Resistor: one leg in column 13, the other in the bottom − rail?
Black wires: GND (column 2) → top − rail, and top − rail → bottom − rail?
Press every part in firmly, plug back in and watch again.
steps.look_for: The LED blinks. You built your first circuit!
steps.watch_out: If it still won't blink, try another LED - they can arrive faulty.

parts_list.note: 2 black, 1 yellow (any colours work - these match the pictures)
